items.followUp: Define empirical formula and write the empirical formula of hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂.

rubric.why: The definition must state that an empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms.
rubric.description: Defines empirical formula as the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the defining idea of a simplest whole-number ratio of atoms, not merely a molecular formula or a formula example.

rubric.why: Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, reduces to the ratio 1:2:1.
rubric.description: Writes the empirical formula of glucose as CH₂O.

modelAnswer: An empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element in a compound.
For glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, divide the subscripts by 6: the empirical formula is CH₂O.

items.followUp: State two observations made in Rutherford’s alpha-particle experiment.

rubric.why: Most alpha particles travelled through the foil without deflection.
rubric.description: States that most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without being deflected.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the observation that most particles passed straight through or were undeflected.

rubric.why: A small number of alpha particles were deflected, and a very small number were reflected backwards.
rubric.description: States that some alpha particles were deflected; a very small number bounced back.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either deflection or backward reflection, provided the response identifies it as an observation.

modelAnswer: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without being deflected.
Some alpha particles were deflected, and a very small number bounced back.

items.followUp: Write the subshell electronic configurations of carbon and fluorine.

rubric.why: Nitrogen has seven electrons: 2 in 1s, 2 in 2s and 3 in 2p.
rubric.description: Gives nitrogen’s subshell electronic configuration as 1s² 2s² 2p³.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the complete, correct configuration.

rubric.why: Oxygen has eight electrons: 2 in 1s, 2 in 2s and 4 in 2p.
rubric.description: Gives oxygen’s subshell electronic configuration as 1s² 2s² 2p⁴.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the complete, correct configuration.

items.followUp: Define a period and a group in the periodic table.

rubric.why: Periods run horizontally across the periodic table.
rubric.description: Defines periods as the horizontal rows of the periodic table.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying periods as horizontal rows.

rubric.why: Groups run vertically down the periodic table.
rubric.description: Defines groups as the vertical columns of the periodic table.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying groups as vertical columns.

modelAnswer: Periods are the horizontal rows of elements in the periodic table.
Groups are the vertical columns of elements in the periodic table.

items.followUp: Define electron affinity and state its general trend down a group.

rubric.why: Electron affinity concerns the energy change when an electron is accepted by an isolated gaseous atom.
rubric.description: Defines electron affinity as the energy released when a neutral gaseous atom accepts an electron to form a negative ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking acceptance of an electron by a gaseous atom with the associated energy change or release.

rubric.why: The attraction for an added electron generally weakens down a group, so electron affinity decreases (becomes less negative).
rubric.description: States that electron affinity generally decreases, or becomes less negative, down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct downward trend.

modelAnswer: Electron affinity is the energy released when a neutral gaseous atom accepts an electron to form a negative ion.
Generally, electron affinity decreases (becomes less negative) down a group.

items.followUp: How many elements are in the 3rd period, and how are they arranged in blocks?

rubric.why: The periodic table is arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
rubric.description: States that elements in the 4th period are arranged in increasing atomic number.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct ordering principle.

rubric.why: The 4th period has 18 elements, with filling across the 4s, 3d and 4p subshells (2, 10 and 6 elements respectively).
rubric.description: Describes the 4th period as 18 elements arranged across the s, d and p blocks, or identifies the 4s, 3d and 4p filling sequence.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct period composition or subshell sequence.

modelAnswer: The elements of the 4th period are arranged in increasing atomic number.
It contains 18 elements: 2 s-block elements, 10 d-block elements and 6 p-block elements; the 4s, 3d and 4p subshells fill in sequence.

items.followUp: Explain why chlorine atoms form a covalent bond with each other, and give the formula of the molecule formed.

rubric.why: Atoms of highly electronegative non-metals can achieve stable outer shells by sharing electrons.
rubric.description: Explains that the atoms share electrons to form a covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons are shared between the atoms.

rubric.why: A chlorine molecule consists of two chlorine atoms joined by a shared pair of electrons.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example, such as Cl₂, of a bond between atoms of the same highly electronegative element.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example, preferably Cl₂.

modelAnswer: Highly electronegative non-metal atoms can form a covalent bond by sharing electrons to complete their outer shells.
For example, two chlorine atoms share a pair of electrons to form a Cl₂ molecule.

items.followUp: Explain why the covalent bond in hydrogen chloride is polar.

rubric.why: A difference in electronegativity causes the bonded atoms to attract the shared electron pair unequally.
rubric.description: States that unequal sharing of the bonding electrons occurs because the bonded atoms have different electronegativities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking unequal sharing to a difference in electronegativity.

rubric.why: Unequal sharing produces partial charges on the bonded atoms, making the bond polar.
rubric.description: Explains that unequal sharing creates partial charges and hence a polar covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying partial charges or correctly naming the bond as polar as a result of unequal sharing.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond becomes polar when bonded atoms have different electronegativities and share the bonding electrons unequally.
The unequal sharing creates partial positive and partial negative charges on the atoms; for example, the H–Cl bond is polar.
